[[File:1506 Arabic transcription - Arte para ligeramente saber la lengua arauiga.jpg|thumb|The ''Arte para ligeramente saber la lengua arauiga'' (1506) by [[Pedro de Alcalá]] uses an innovative system for transcribing [[Andalusian Arabic]] that has been called "the first Western system of Arabic scientific transcription" by [[Federico Corriente]].<ref>[https://revistas.ucm.es/index.php/ILUR/article/view/75206/4564456557261 «La lengua de la gente común y no los priores de la gramática arábiga».La Doctrina christiana en lengua arábiga y castellana (1566) de Martín Pérez de Ayala], Teresa Soto González, University of Salamanca {{in lang|es}}</ref>]]

'''Andalusi Arabic''' or '''Andalusian Arabic''' ({{Langx|ar|اللهجة العربية الأندلسية|al-lahja al-ʿarabiyya al-ʾandalusiyya}}) was a [[varieties of Arabic|variety or varieties of Arabic]]{{Efn|Spanish Arabist and lexicographer [[Federico Corriente]] insisted on describing Andalusi Arabic as a "dialect bundle" in which "the common core was predominant and the local features, minimal."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Corriente |first=Federico |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3ZQOAAAAYAAJ |title=A Grammatical Sketch of the Spanish Arabic Dialect Bundle |date=1977 |publisher=Instituto Hispano-Arabe de Cultura |isbn=978-84-600-0737-1 |language=en}}</ref> Within this dialect bundle, there were regional variations as well as higher and lower colloquial [[Register (sociolinguistics)|registers]].<ref name=":10" />}} spoken mainly from the 8th to the 15th century in [[Al-Andalus]], the regions of the [[Iberian Peninsula]] under the [[Islamic history|Muslim rule]].

Arabic spread gradually over the centuries of Muslim rule in Iberia, primarily through conversion to [[Islam]], although it was also learned and spoken by Christians and Jews. Arabic became the [[Official language|language of administration]] and was the primary language of [[Literature of al-Andalus|literature produced in al-Andalus]]; the Andalusi vernacular was distinct among medieval Arabic vernaculars in that it was used in poetry, in ''[[zajal]]'' and the ''[[kharja]]s'' of ''[[Muwashshah|muwaššaḥāt]]''.

Arabic in al-Andalus existed largely in a situation of [[Multilingualism|bilingualism]] with [[Andalusi Romance]] (known popularly as ''Mozarabic'') until the 13th century. Arabic in Iberia was also characterized by [[diglossia]]: in addition to standard written Arabic, spoken varieties could be subdivided into an urban, educated [[idiolect]] and a register of the less-privileged masses.

After the [[Granada War|fall of Granada]] in 1492, the Catholic rulers suppressed the use of Arabic, persecuting its speakers, passing policies against its use (such as the {{Interlanguage link|Pragmática Sanción de 1567|es}}, which led directly to the [[Rebellion of the Alpujarras (1568–1571)|Rebellion of the Alpujarras]]), and [[expulsion of the Moriscos|expelling the Moriscos]] in the early 17th century, after which Arabic became an [[extinct language]] in Iberia. An Andalusi variety of Arabic continued to be spoken to some degree in North Africa after the expulsion, and it was notably preserved in [[Andalusi classical music]] traditions in North Africa. Andalusi speakers influenced the speech of those [[Maghreb]]i communities into which they fled and assimilated.

Spoken Andalusi Arabic had distinct features. It is unique among colloquial dialects in retaining from Standard Arabic the [[Arabic verbs#Voice|internal passive voice]] through vocalization. Through contact with [[Andalusi Romance|Romance]], spoken Andalusi Arabic adopted the phonemes {{IPAslink|p}} and {{IPAslink|tʃ}}. Like the other Iberian languages, Andalusi lacked [[vowel length]] but had [[Stress (linguistics)|stress]] instead (e.g. ''Andalusí'' in place of ''Andalusī''). A feature shared with [[Maghrebi Arabic]] was that the first-person [[Imperfective aspect|imperfect]] was marked with the prefix ''n-'' ({{Lang|xaa|نلعب}} ''nalʿab'' 'I play') like the plural in Standard Arabic, necessitating an analogical imperfect first-person plural, constructed with the suffix ''-ū'' ({{Lang|xaa|نلعبوا}} ''nalʿabū'' 'we play'). A feature characteristic of it was the extensive [[imala]] that transformed alif into an /e/ or /i/ (e.g. ''al-kirā'' ("rent") > ''al-kirē'' > Spanish "''alquiler''").

==History==

=== Origins ===
The [[Muslim conquest of Spain]] in 711, about a century after the death of [[Muhammad]], involved a few thousand Arab tribesmen<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |url=https://brill.com/edcollbook/title/3349 |title=A Descriptive and Comparative Grammar of Andalusi Arabic |date=1977-01-01 |publisher=Brill |isbn=978-90-04-23027-9 |editor-last=University of Zaragoza |editor-first= |language=en}}</ref> and a much larger number of partially Arabicized [[Amazigh]], many of whom spoke little to no [[Arabic]].<ref name=":10">{{Cite book |last1=López-Morillas |first1=Consuelo |title=The literature of Al-Andalus |date=2012 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-17787-0 |editor-last=Menocal |editor-first=María Rosa |chapter=Language |oclc=819159086 |editor-last2=Scheindlin |editor-first2=Raymond P. |editor-last3=Sells |editor-first3=Michael}}</ref> According to Consuelo López-Morillas, "this population sowed the seeds of what was to grow into an indigenous Andalusi Arabic."<ref name=":10" />

Unlike the [[Visigothic Kingdom|Visigothic conquest of Hispania]], through which [[Latin]] remained the dominant language, the Muslim conquest brought a language that was a "vehicle for a higher culture, a literate and literary civilization."<ref name=":10" />

=== Spread ===

Over the centuries, Arabic spread gradually in al-Andalus, primarily through conversion to [[Islam]].<ref name=":5">López-Morillas, Consuelo (2000). "Language". The literature of Al-Andalus. New York: Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/CHOL9780521471596.004. ISBN 9781139177870.</ref> While [[Paul Albar|Alvarus of Cordoba]] lamented in the 9th century that Christians were no longer using Latin, [[Richard Bulliet]] estimates that only 50% of the population of al-Andalus had converted to Islam by the death of [[Abd al-Rahman III]] in 961, and 80% by 1100.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Bulliet |first=Richard W. |date=1979-12-31 |title=Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674732810 |publisher=De Gruyter |doi=10.4159/harvard.9780674732810|isbn=978-0-674-73280-3 }} ''Cited in'' {{Citation |last=Morillas |first=Consuelo López |title=Language |date=2000-08-31 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/CBO9781139177870A009/type/book_part |work=The Literature of Al-Andalus |pages=31–59 |editor-last=Menocal |editor-first=María Rosa |access-date=2023-02-17 |edition=1 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/chol9780521471596.004 |isbn=978-0-521-47159-6 |editor2-last=Scheindlin |editor2-first=Raymond P. |editor3-last=Sells |editor3-first=Michael|url-access=subscription }}</ref> By about 1260, Muslim territories in Iberia were reduced to the [[Emirate of Granada]], in which more than 90% of the population had converted to Islam and Arabic-Romance bilingualism seems to have disappeared.<ref name=":3" />[[File:Letter (T-S 8J18.5).jpg|thumb|A letter handwritten in [[Judeo-Arabic dialects|Judeo-Arabic]] by [[Judah Halevi|Judah ha-Levi]] (1075–1141). While Muslims did not write in vernacular registers of Arabic, Andalusi Jews would write in colloquial Arabic with [[Hebrew alphabet|Hebrew script]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=López-Morillas |first=Consuelo |title=The literature of Al-Andalus |date=2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |others=Maria Rosa Menocal, Raymond P. Scheindlin, Michael Anthony Sells |isbn=978-1-139-17787-0 |location=New York |chapter=Chapter 2: Language |oclc=794678936}}</ref>]]
The colloquial Arabic of al-Andalus was prominent among the [[varieties of Arabic]] of its time in its use for literary purposes, especially in ''[[zajal]]'' poetry and [[proverb]]s and [[aphorism]]s.<ref name=":10" />

=== Demise ===
After the [[Granada War|Fall of Granada]] in 1492, Cardinal [[Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros]] oversaw the forced mass conversion of the population in the [[Spanish Inquisition]] and the burning of Andalusi manuscripts in Granada.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Francisco, Cardinal Jiménez de Cisneros {{!}} Spanish cardinal |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Francisco-Cardenal-Jimenez-de-Cisneros |access-date=2020-08-06 |website=Encyclopedia Britannica |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=CENSORSHIP AND BOOK PRODUCTION IN SPAIN DURING THE AGE OF THE INCUNABULA |url=http://www.lehman.edu/ciberletras/v06/tofino.html |access-date=2020-08-06 |website=www.lehman.edu}}</ref> In 1502, the Muslims of Granada were forced to choose between conversion and exile; those who converted became known as the [[Morisco]]s. In 1526, [[Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor|Charles V]] (Charles I of Spain)—issued an edict against "heresy" (e.g. Muslim practices by "New Christians"), including the use of Arabic, extending the restriction to Muslims throughout the rest of Spain, the [[Mudéjar]]s. The Moriscos managed to get this suspended for forty years by the payment of a large sum (80,000 ducados).<ref>Lea, pp. 215-6</ref> King [[Philip II of Spain]]'s ''{{Interlanguage link|Pragmática Sanción de 1567|es}}'' finally banned the use of Arabic throughout Spain—forbidding Moriscos from the [[language death|use of Arabic on all occasions]], formal and informal, speaking and writing—leading directly to the [[Rebellion of the Alpujarras (1568–71)]].<ref>Lea, p.227</ref> Still, Andalusi Arabic remained in use in certain areas of Spain (particularly the inner regions of [[Kingdom of Valencia|Valencia]] and [[Kingdom of Aragon|Aragon]])<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Barceló |first1=Carmen |title=Archivos moriscos : textos árabes de la minoría islámica valenciana 1401-1608 |last2=Labarta |first2=Ana |date=2009 |publisher=Universitat de València |isbn=978-84-370-7384-2 |oclc=804262422}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fournel-Guerin |first=Jacqueline |date=1979 |title=Le livre et la civilisation écrite dans la communauté morisque aragonaise (1540-1620) |url=https://www.persee.fr/doc/casa_0076-230x_1979_num_15_1_2299 |journal=Mélanges de la Casa de Velázquez |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=241–259 |doi=10.3406/casa.1979.2299|doi-access=free }}</ref> until the final [[expulsion of the Moriscos]] at the beginning of the 17th century.<ref name="Brill">[[Kees Versteegh]], et al.: ''Encyclopedia of Arabic Language and Linguistics'', [[Brill Publishers]], 2006.</ref>

=== Legacy ===
Andalusi Arabic is still used in [[Andalusi classical music]] and has significantly influenced the dialects of such towns as [[Sfax]] in Tunisia, [[Rabat]], [[Salé]], [[Fès]], [[Tétouan]] and [[Tangier]] in Morocco, [[Nedroma]], [[Tlemcen]], [[Blida]], [[Jijel]], and [[Cherchell]] in Algeria. Andalusi Arabic also influenced [[Andalusi Romance]] ("Mozarabic"), [[Spanish language|Spanish]], [[Judaeo-Spanish]] varieties, [[Catalan language|Catalan]], [[Portuguese language|Portuguese]], and [[Algerian Arabic|Algerian]], [[Moroccan Arabic|Moroccan]],and [[Tunisian Arabic|Tunisian]] Arabics.

==Sociolinguistic features ==

=== Prestige ===
Under Muslim rule, Arabic became a [[Stratum (linguistics)|superstrate]], [[Prestige (sociolinguistics)|prestige]] language and the dominant medium of [[Literature of al-Andalus|literary]] and intellectual expression in the southern half of the peninsula from the 8th century to the 13th century.<ref name=":10" /> Consuelo Lopez-Morillas notes that poetic genres such as ''[[zajal]]'' and the popular literature of proverbs and aphorisms demonstrate that, among speakers of Andalusi Arabic, there was a "consciousness of, and even pride in, the distinctiveness of the dialect, its suppleness and expressivity."<ref name=":10" />

=== Multilingualism and language contact ===

==== Romance ====
Arabic in al-Andalus existed largely in a situation of [[Multilingualism|bilingualism]] with [[Andalusi Romance|Romance]] until the 13th century,<ref name=":0" /> when the [[Almohad Caliphate|Almohad]] expansion into Iberia led to the flight of Christians living under Muslim rule in the south of Iberia northward to territories under Christian rule<ref name=":23">{{Cite book |last=Bennison |first=Amira K. |author-link=Amira Bennison |title=The Almoravid and Almohad Empires |publisher=Edinburgh University Press |year=2016 |isbn=9780748646821}}</ref>{{Rp|pages=173–174}} and to the reduction of territory under Muslim rule to the [[Emirate of Granada]] following a sequence of Christian conquests of Muslim cities.<ref name=":3" />

Of the approximately 600 known secular Arabic ''[[Muwashshah|muwaššaḥāt]]'', there about 50 with ''[[kharja]]s'' in [[Andalusi Romance]] or containing some Romance words or elements.<ref name=":102">{{Cite book |last1=Menocal |first1=María Rosa |title=The literature of al-Andalus |last2=Scheindlin |first2=Raymond P. |last3=Sells |first3=Micheal |date=2012 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-17787-0 |oclc=819159086}}</ref>{{Rp|page=185}}

The influence of Romance on Andalusi Arabic was especially pronounced in situations of daily Arabic-Romance [[Language contact|contact]]. For example, an Arabic letter written by a Valencian Morisco in 1595 contained constructions such as {{Transliteration|xaa|taʿmál alburšíblī}} ('do what is possible,' constructed with the Arabic verb {{Lang|ar|تعمل}} 'you do,' the Arabic definitive article {{Lang|ar|الـ}} 'the' and the Romance {{Transliteration|mxi|buršíblī}} cognate of English 'possible') and {{Transliteration|xaa|aquštiš matáʿī}} ('at a cost to me,' with the Romance {{Transliteration|mxi|aquštiš}} 'at a cost' and the Arabic personal possessive {{Lang|ar|متاعي}} 'my').<ref name=":5" />

The [[influence of Arabic on Spanish]] resulting from this linguistic contact has been thoroughly studied, but Romance also reciprocally influenced Andalusi Arabic.<ref name=":5" /> Dialectical features of Andalusi Arabic owing to Arabic-Romance bilingualism and contact include of the adoption of the phonemes {{IPAslink|p}} and {{IPAslink|tʃ}}; the substitution of the traditional Arabic [[vowel length]] for the Iberian syllabic [[Stress (linguistics)|stress]] (e.g. ''Andalusí'' in place of ''Andalusī''); and the change of [[Grammatical gender|gender]] of some nouns to corresponding the gender in Romance, such as the feminine Arabic nouns ''ʿayn'' ({{Lang|ar|عين}} 'eye') and ''shams'' ({{Lang|ar|شمس}} 'sun'), which became masculine in al-Andalus, matching ''ojo'' and ''sol''.<ref name=":5" />

==== Hebrew ====
Arabic also coexisted with [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]], and Arabic features and traditions had a major impact on Jewish poetry in Iberia.<ref name=":5" /> There is evidence that [[code-switching]] was commonplace among bilingual populations in al-Andalus.<ref name=":5" /> About half of the corpus of the more than 250 known ''[[Muwashshah|muwaššaḥāt]]'' in [[Biblical Hebrew|Hebrew]] have ''[[kharja]]s'' in Arabic, and some there are some ''kharjas'' with a mix of Arabic and Hebrew.<ref name=":102"/>{{Rp|page=185}}

==== {{Transliteration|ar|al-lisān al-gharbī}} ====
It also had some contact with [[Berber languages]] or {{Transliteration|ar|al-lisān al-gharbī}} ({{Lang|ar|اللسان الغربي}} 'the western tongue') in periods of Berber rule, particularly under the Almoravids<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gómez |first1=Emilio García |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EBMGzgEACAAJ |title=Un eclipse de la poesía en Sevilla: la época almorávide |last2=Palencia |first2=Ángel González |date=1945 |publisher=Real Academia Española |language=es}}</ref> and Almohads,<ref name=":032">{{Citation |title=The Preaching of the Almohads: Loyalty and Resistance across the Strait of Gibraltar |date=2013-01-01 |work=Spanning the Strait |pages=71–101 |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1163/9789004256644_004 |access-date=2023-02-13 |publisher=BRILL |doi=10.1163/9789004256644_004 |isbn=9789004256644 |last1=Jones |first1=Linda G. |url-access=subscription }}</ref> though [[Federico Corriente]] identified only about 15 Berberisms that entered Andalusi Arabic speech.<ref name=":10" />

=== Diglossia ===
It was also characterized by [[diglossia]]: in addition to standard written Arabic, spoken varieties could be subdivided into an urban, educated [[idiolect]] and a register of the less-privileged masses.<ref name=":0" />

==Linguistic features ==
Many features of Andalusi Arabic have been reconstructed by [[Arabist]]s using Hispano-Arabic texts (such as the ''[[zajal|azjāl]]'' of [[ibn Quzman]], [[Abu al-Hasan al-Shushtari|al-Shushtari]] and others) composed in Arabic with varying degrees of deviation from classical norms, augmented by further information from the manner in which the Arabic script was used to transliterate Romance words. The first complete linguistic description of Andalusi Arabic was given by the Spanish Arabist [[Federico Corriente]], who drew on the ''[[Appendix Probi]]'', ''[[zajal]]'' poetry, proverbs and aphorisms, the work of the 16th century lexicographer [[Pedro de Alcalá]], and Andalusi letters found in the [[Cairo Geniza]].<ref name=":10" />

=== Lexicography ===

==== Romance loanwords ====
As Arabisms moved into varieties of Iberian Romance over time, Andalusi Arabic borrowed widely from the Romance lexicon.<ref name=":5" /> Corriente observes three periods in which Romance words entered Arabic, as Romance shifted from a substratum to an adstratum to a superstratum with respect to Arabic.<ref name=":5" /> Semantic fields such as plant and animal names, domestic objects, and agriculture received the most loanwords.<ref name=":5" /> Sometimes both the Romance and Arabic words were used, such as the words {{Transliteration|xaa|imlíq}} (from {{lang|roa-ES|UMBILICU}}) and {{Transliteration|xaa|surra}} ({{Lang|ar|سُرَّة}}) for [[navel]]; Consuelo Lopez-Morillas recalls "the many households made up of Hispano-Roman women and Arab men."<ref name=":5" /> Once subsumed into Arabic morphological patterns, Romance loanwords became difficult to distinguish as such. For example, {{Transliteration|xaa|nibšāriuh}} (from {{lang|roa-ES|aniversario}} 'anniversary' or 'birthday') was made plural as {{Transliteration|xaa|nibšāriyāt}} and {{Transliteration|xaa|lubb}} (from {{lang|roa-ES|lobo}} 'wolf') became a [[Broken plural#Arabic|broken plural]] as {{Transliteration|xaa|lababah}}.<ref name=":5" /> Romance loanwords were used in Andalusi Arabic through the end of Muslim rule in Iberia, even after [[Emirate of Granada|Granada]] had been monolingually arabophone for two centuries.<ref name=":5" />

==== Berber loanwords ====
The lexical impact of [[Berber languages|Berber language]] on Andalusi Arabic appears to be considerably less than that of Romance and very small in proportion to the extensive Berber presence in al-Andalus.<ref name=":5" /> Corriente identified about 15 Berberisms that entered Andalusi Arabic, only a few of which were still in use in the early 16th century.<ref name=":5" />

The [[phoneme]] represented by the letter ق in texts is a point of contention. The letter, which in Classical Arabic represented either a voiceless pharyngealized [[velar stop]] or a voiceless [[uvular stop]], most likely represented some kind of post-alveolar affricate or [[velar plosive]] in Andalusi Arabic. Federico Corriente presents the case that ق most often represented {{IPA|/q/}}, sometimes {{IPA|/k/}}, and marginally {{IPA|/ɡ/}} based on a plethora of surviving Andalusi writings and Romance transcriptions of Andalusi Arabic words.<ref name="Corriente 2013 30–31">{{Harvcoltxt|Corriente|2013|pp=30–31}}</ref>

The vowel system was subject to a heavy amount of fronting and raising, a phenomenon known as ''[[imāla]]'', causing {{IPA|/a(ː)/}} to be raised, probably to {{IPAblink|ɛ}} or {{IPAblink|e}} and, particularly with short vowels, {{IPAblink|ɪ}} in certain circumstances, particularly when i-mutation was possible.

Contact with native [[Romance languages|Romance speakers]] led to the introduction of the phonemes {{IPAslink|p}}, {{IPAslink|ɡ}} and, possibly, the affricate {{IPAslink|tʃ}} from [[loanword]]s.

[[Monophthongization]] led to the disappearance of certain [[diphthong]]s such as {{IPA|/aw/}} and {{IPA|/aj/}} which were leveled to {{IPAslink|oː}} and {{IPAslink|eː}}, respectively, though Colin hypothesizes that these diphthongs remained in the more [[mesolect]]al registers influenced by the Classical language. Alternatively in higher registers, {{IPAblink|e}} and {{IPAblink|o}} were only allophones of {{IPAslink|i}} and {{IPAslink|u}} respectively, while diphthongs were mostly resistant to monophthongization.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Corriente|2013|pp=5–6, 7–9}}</ref> However, {{IPAslink|a}} could turn into {{IPAblink|e}} or {{IPAblink|i}} via ''imāla''.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Corriente|2013|p=2}}</ref> In the presence of velar or pharyngeal contour, {{IPAslink|a}} was backed into {{IPAblink|ɑ}} and sometimes even rounded into {{IPAblink|o}} or {{IPAblink|u}}, or even {{IPAblink|ɒ}}. This is evidenced by occasional Romance or even local Arabic transcription of {{IPAslink|a}} as {{IPAblink|o}} or {{IPAblink|u}}.<ref>{{Harvcoltxt|Corriente|2013|pp=4–5}}</ref>

There was a fair amount of compensatory lengthening involved where a loss of consonantal gemination lengthened the preceding vowel, whence the transformation of {{lang|ar|عشّ}} <!--don't use {{IPA-ar}}-->{{IPA|/ʕuʃ(ʃ)/}} ("nest") into {{lang|ar|عوش}} <!--don't use {{IPA-ar}}-->{{IPA|/ʕuːʃ/}}.

New phonemes introduced into Andalusi Arabic, such as {{IPA|/p/}} and {{IPA|/t͡ʃ/}} were often written as geminated {{lang|ar|بّ}} and {{lang|ar|جّ}} respectively. This would later be carried over into [[Aljamiado]], in which {{IPA|/p/}} and {{IPA|/t͡ʃ/}} in Romance languages would be transcribed with the above letters, each containing a [[shadda]].

===Syntax ===

==== Passive voice ====
Andalusi Arabic is uniquely conservative among colloquial Arabic dialects for retaining the internal [[passive voice]] ({{Lang|ar|صيغة المجهول}} {{lang|ar-Latn|sighatu l-majhūl}}) of [[Arabic verbs#Voice|Standard Arabic verbs]], using the same stem of the active voice verb with different vocalization. The passive voice is expressed in the past or perfect tense with [[Arabic diacritics#Kasrah|kasra]] (/i/) on the last syllable and [[Arabic diacritics#Ḍammah|damma]] (/u/) on all other syllables, and in the imperfect tense with damma /u/ on the personal subject prefix—the first syllable—and [[Arabic diacritics#Fatḥah|fatḥah]] /a/ on the following syllables.<ref>{{Cite book |last=University of Zaragoza |first=Institute of Islamic Studies |url=http://worldcat.org/oclc/1259249610 |title=A descriptive and comparative grammar of Andalusi Arabic |date=2012 |publisher=Brill |isbn=978-1-283-63484-7 |oclc=1259249610}}</ref>{{Rp|page=89}}

==== Noun gender ====
Some nouns in Andalusi Arabic shifted [[Gender (linguistics)|gender]] to match the gender of corresponding terms in Romance, such as the feminine Arabic nouns ''ʿayn'' ({{Lang|ar|عين}} 'eye') and ''shams'' ({{Lang|ar|شمس}} 'sun'), which became masculine in al-Andalus, matching ''ojo'' and ''sol''.<ref name=":5" />

=== Morphology ===
Gender distinction in second-person pronouns and verbs was abandoned.<ref name=":5" />

There were about twenty suffixes from Romance that were attached to Arabic bases.<ref name=":5" />

The ''{{transliteration|ar|ALA|-an}}'' which, in Classical Arabic, marked a noun as indefinite [[accusative case]] (see [[nunation]]), became an indeclinable [[conjunctive]] particle, as in ibn Quzmān's expression ''{{transliteration|xaa|rajul-an 'ashīq}}''.

The unconjugated prepositive negative particle ''{{transliteration|xaa|lis}}'' developed out of the classical verb ''{{transliteration|ar|ALA|lays-a}}''.

The [[derivational morphology]] of the verbal system was substantially altered. One example is the initial ''n-'' on verbs in the [[first person singular]], a feature shared by many Maghrebi varieties. Likewise the form V pattern of ''{{transliteration|ar|ALA|tafaʻʻal-a}}'' ({{lang|ar|تَفَعَّلَ}}) was altered by [[epenthesis]]{{Dubious|date=June 2021|reason=at least superficially more like [[Metathesis (linguistics)|metathesis]]. If not, explanation is needed.}} to ''{{transliteration|xaa|atfa``al}}'' ({{lang|xaa|أتْفَعَّل}}).

Andalusi Arabic developed a contingent/subjunctive [[Grammatical mood|mood]] (after a [[Conditional sentence|protasis]] with the conditional particle ''{{transliteration|ar|ALA|law}}''<span style="margin-left:1px">)</span> consisting of the imperfect (prefix) form of a verb, preceded by either ''{{transliteration|xaa|kān}}'' or ''{{transliteration|xaa|kīn}}'' (depending on the register of the speech in question), of which the final ''{{transliteration|ar|ALA|-n}}'' was normally assimilated by preformatives ''{{transliteration|xaa|y-}}'' and ''{{transliteration|xaa|t-}}''. == Recorded evidence ==
The oldest evidence of Andalusi Arabic utterances can be dated from the 10th and 11th century, in isolated quotes, both in [[prose]] and [[stanza]]ic Classical Andalusi poems (''[[muwashshah]]at''), and then, from the 11th century on, in stanzaic dialectal poems (''zajal'') and dialectal proverb collections.<ref name="Brill" />

Substantial material on late Granadan Arabic survives in the work of [[Pedro de Alcalá]]—the ''[[Vocabulista aravigo en letra castellana]]''<ref>{{Cite web |title=Vocabulista aravigo en letra castellana|url=http://bdh-rd.bne.es/viewer.vm?id=0000090897|access-date=2023-04-02 |website=Biblioteca Digital Hispánica}}</ref> and [[Arte para ligeramente saber lengua araviga|''Arte para ligeramente saber la lengua araviga'']],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Arte para ligeramẽte saber la lẽgua arauiga |url=http://bdh-rd.bne.es/viewer.vm?id=0000037465&page=1 |access-date=2023-04-02 |website=Biblioteca Digital Hispánica}}</ref> both published in 1505 to explain the language of the conquered to the conquerors following the [[Granada War|Fall of Granada]].<ref name=":5" />

Its last documents are a few business records and one letter written at the beginning of the 17th century in [[Valencia]].<ref name="Brill" />
